title: [STORY] Cold open — Ostler Street
vo:
Every evening, for more than a century, someone in a city like this walked out at dusk with a ladder and a long pole, and gave the street its night.
Ida isn't real, and her street has no name. But her job was real.
This channel is about jobs like hers: the work people do, and what happens to it when machines learn to do it. Ida lights a lamp for each of those jobs. Tonight, she starts with her own.
dia: *IDA (soft, to no one):* Evening, old street.

title: [HISTORY] Title + "Pall Mall, 1807"
vo:
London, 1807. On one street, Pall Mall, a row of lamps burning coal gas was lit. It is remembered as the first street in the world lit that way.
The idea spread fast. By the 1820s, London had more than forty thousand gas lamps, along some two hundred and fifteen miles of street.
And every one of those lamps needed a person, every dusk and every dawn.

title: [HISTORY] The round
vo:
That person's shift was called a round: dozens of lamps along a fixed route, lit at dusk and put out at dawn. In between, you cleaned the glass and reported the broken ones.
Rain, fog or frost, the lamps had to be lit. It was, almost entirely, one task, repeated. Remember that. It matters later.

title: [STORY] "Not yet… not yet."
vo: Ida's watch runs seven minutes slow. She knows it. The city's clock is moving on.
dia: *IDA (under her breath, hurrying):* Not yet… not yet.

title: [HISTORY] The white wave
vo:
Then came a different kind of light. In 1878, Paris strung sixty-four electric arc lamps along and around the Avenue de l'Opéra. They needed nobody on a ladder.
It was a slow tide, not a single night: a white lamp on the main avenue, a few more on the side streets, and every round got a little shorter.

title: [HISTORY] New York, April 1907
vo:
In April 1907, New York's lamplighters went on strike for union recognition and better pay. Parts of the city went dark. Police officers were sent out to light the lamps, some climbing the posts with matches.
Within about a week, the men were back at work. A strike only works if the city can't do without you, and every year the city could do a little more without them.

title: [HISTORY] [SHORTS S1] "London's last lamplighters"
vo:
Here is what most people don't know. London still has gas street lamps, in Covent Garden, along the Mall, outside palaces and theatres.
British Gas says its team looked after about eleven hundred of them in 2023. That team is five people. Five lamplighters.
They don't carry fire anymore. Most lamps run on small clockwork timers, and every two weeks someone climbs up to wind the clock and check the lamp.

title: [HISTORY] [SHORTS S3] From lamps to lifts: "One job in 270"
vo:
Lamplighting was one job built almost entirely around one task, and that is exactly the kind of job a machine can take whole.
The next one came indoors. U.S. census counts show about thirteen thousand elevator operators in 1900, and nearly a hundred thousand by 1950. Then elevators began to run themselves. By 1970, thirty-seven thousand were left.
The economist James Bessen followed about two hundred and seventy occupations from the 1950 census to 2010. Many shrank or changed. Only one disappeared mainly because of automation: the elevator operator.

title: [HISTORY] The office of 1970
vo:
The same census tables tell a second story. Telephone operators: about nineteen thousand in 1900, about four hundred and twenty thousand by 1970. Stenographers, typists and secretaries, counted together: from about a hundred and thirty thousand to nearly four million.
In 1970, those were the jobs of the modern office.

title: [STORY] Bridge — the office lights
vo: Ida's lamp still burns at the end of the street. Behind it, the office lights are on.

title: [TODAY] [SHORTS S2] "Today's shortest rounds"
vo:
In the 1960s, the job on its way out was the elevator operator. Today, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics has a list of its own: the jobs it projects will shrink fastest between 2025 and 2035.
At the top, word processors and typists: down thirty-four percent. Telephone operators, down twenty-eight. Switchboard operators and data entry keyers, down about a quarter. Telemarketers, down a fifth.
Not the same technology. The same pattern: one task, repeated, and a machine that can repeat it.

title: [TODAY] AI in the forecast
vo: The Bureau names AI in its forecasts. In its 2023 to 2033 projections, it expected AI to mostly affect jobs whose core tasks generative AI can most easily copy. Customer service representatives: down five percent. Auto damage appraisers: down nine. Claims adjusters: down about four.

title: [TODAY] Jobs that grow
vo:
Some jobs grow. In that same round, software developers: up almost eighteen percent. In the newest projections, for 2025 to 2035: nurse practitioners up forty-one, solar installers up more than thirty-six, data scientists up about thirty-five.
Some jobs end. Some change. Some are new.

title: [TODAY] The same clock
vo:
To compare speeds fairly, put them on the same clock: change over ten years.
Elevator operators, counted by the census: down almost a fifth in the 1950s, then by half in the 1960s. Word processors and typists, projected by the Bureau: down about a third over the next ten years.
One is history, the other a forecast. The census counted people; the Bureau counts jobs. But the size is of the same order.
So what is different this time? The elevator was one machine replacing one job in one kind of building. AI reaches into many office and knowledge jobs at once: writing, answering, checking, coding. The pattern is old. The reach is new. One forecast, one technology, and its case studies run from call centres to insurance offices to law firms.

title: [TODAY] Why these jobs
vo: The Bureau says why. Across office and administrative support, it projects employment to fall about four percent, as automation tools, including those powered by AI, take on more of the work. Meanwhile total U.S. employment is projected to grow about three and a half percent.

title: [TODAY] Jobs that change
vo:
Remember Bessen's two hundred and seventy jobs: machines mostly took over tasks, not whole jobs. Many jobs that AI touches are still growing. Take lawyers. In that 2023 to 2033 round, the Bureau expected AI to speed up parts of legal work, but said its output still needs detailed review by lawyers. Lawyers were projected to grow about five percent, close to the four percent average for all jobs. Paralegals, about one percent. In finance, the same round had credit analysts down about four percent, but financial analysts up almost ten.
The work changes. The job remains.

title: [TODAY] [SHORTS S4 — đề xuất] An early signal
vo:
One early warning sign. Researchers at Stanford's Digital Economy Lab looked at payroll data through June 2026. Workers aged twenty-two to twenty-five in the jobs most exposed to AI were employed at about nineteen percent below where they would otherwise be, mostly because fewer were hired. More experienced workers showed no such gap.
The researchers call it an early signal, not proof that AI caused it.

title: [TODAY] Not verdicts
vo: Forecasts are not verdicts. Some of these jobs will end, many will change, and new ones will appear that nobody has a name for yet. These numbers describe a whole country, not any one person's future. But they tell us where to look. The lamplighters had no list like this. We do.

title: [STORY] Ida lights a lamp
vo:
Ida lights one lamp for every job that ends this way. Tonight, her second lamp is for the elevator operators.
Cas holds the ladder. He will grow up in the white city, but he knows what a lamp is for.
Every era has its last lamplighters. So here is the question this channel will keep asking:
Who are the last lamplighters of our time?
